content.text: An Anemic Domain Model has entities named after business concepts but no behavior: public getters and setters, with every rule living in service classes. Martin Fowler calls it an anti-pattern because you pay for a domain model and get procedural code, and every rule holds only for callers that remember to use the right service. Put rules in the entity that owns the data, keep services thin, and keep plain data classes for simple CRUD.
Support added a "goodwill gift" button last sprint. The endpoint loads the order, calls

and saves. It passed review and its tests. A week later finance finds shipped orders with new lines, and totals that no longer match those lines. The rule "no changes after payment" was there all along, in
, which also recalculates the total. The new endpoint just never called it, and nothing in
The belief: entities are data. They should be plain classes with public properties that mirror the tables, and business rules belong in service classes:
. Keeping data and logic apart is clean separation of concerns.

It's an easy belief to pick up. Scaffolding tools and many tutorials generate entities as property bags, and older versions of Entity Framework required collections that any caller could add to. Many experienced designers recommend a service layer on top of the domain model, and Fowler notes that this causes confusion. And for a simple CRUD service, Microsoft's .NET microservices guide says plain data entities aren't an anti-pattern at all.
The half-truth: services have a real job, and simple CRUD doesn't need rich entities. But once the rules are many and keep changing, moving them out of the entities leaves the data unguarded.
It looks like a domain model

starts with how convincing it looks: objects "named after the nouns in the domain space", connected with real relationships. The catch is "that there is hardly any behavior on these objects, making them little more than bags of getters and setters." A set of service objects "capture all the domain logic, carrying out all the computation and updating the model objects with the results." His verdict on the cost: anemic models "incur all of the costs of a domain model, without yielding any of the benefits." You still map objects to tables, and what you get back is procedural code, a set of Transaction Scripts.
Rules in services are rules you can skip

Microsoft's guide states the alternative plainly: "Domain entities must implement behavior in addition to implementing data attributes," and "The entity's methods take care of the invariants and rules of the entity instead of having those rules spread across the application layer." Its validation chapter adds that "Domain entities should always be valid entities," because "many bugs occur because objects are in a state they should never have been in."

holds only where someone remembered to call the service. Every new entry point, such as an admin endpoint, a background job, a message handler or a data fix, has to rediscover the rule. When the entity enforces it, there's no path around it.

A rich model doesn't remove services. Fowler quotes Eric Evans on the application layer: it "is kept thin. It does not contain business rules or knowledge, but only coordinates tasks and delegates work to collaborations of domain objects in the next layer down." Loading the order, saving it and sending the confirmation email are coordination. Deciding whether a line can be added is a business rule. Fowler also stresses that this doesn't mix persistence into the domain: the logic in a domain object is "domain logic - validations, calculations, business rules".
EF Core doesn't need public setters
The ORM argument is mostly history. Microsoft's guide notes that since EF Core 1.1 entities can use plain fields and private property setters, and a collection can be exposed as
, with EF Core reading and writing the field. The database mapping lives in the persistence layer, so the entity stays a plain C# class.
The fix: let the entity guard its own rules

rows.text: Entities are data; rules go in services
Microsoft: entities implement behavior, and their methods guard the invariants
A service layer means entities without behavior
Evans: the application layer is thin and delegates to domain objects
Rich entities mix persistence into the domain
Fowler: domain objects hold domain logic; persistence stays in its own layer
Since EF Core 1.1: private setters, fields, and read-only collections backed by fields
For a simple CRUD service, Microsoft says they're not an anti-pattern

blocks.title: Every public setter is a way around the rules

content.text: A rule enforced in a service holds only for code that calls that service. Admin tools, jobs, imports and tests that build objects by hand all bypass it, and the first symptom is data that should be impossible: a shipped order with new lines, or a total that doesn't match. By then the bad rows are already in the database.

blocks.title: Find the methods that belong somewhere else

content.text: Search for assignments to an entity's properties outside the entity itself, such as
. A service method that takes an entity as its first parameter and changes its state is usually a method looking for its class.

Microsoft's guide recommends two-step validation: field-level checks such as required fields and formats on the incoming command or DTO, and domain-level rules inside the entities. The first gives users quick feedback; the second keeps the model valid whatever path the data took.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Pick one entity with real rules

content.text: Start where bugs cluster, such as orders, payments or bookings. List every rule about it that lives in a service, a controller or a validator.

items.text: An anemic model has the shape of a domain model without its behavior: all the mapping cost, none of the protection.
A rule in a service holds only for callers that use that service; a rule in the entity holds for everyone.
Services coordinate, entities decide; Evans's application layer is deliberately thin.
EF Core supports private setters and read-only collections, so persistence is no excuse for public setters.
Plain data entities are fine for simple CRUD; choose rich entities where rules are many and keep changing.
